name: Iris Garcia

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I buy gloves, dressings and syringes for Meridian Medical Supply, a distributor that serves clinics, care homes and two hospitals. I worked in a pharmacy for years, then moved into buying six years ago, so I'm still the junior beside Katrin, our senior buyer. My mornings are stock reports and supplier calls, afternoons are quotes and chasing delays. What wears me out is a shortage, when every clinic phones at once.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I love it when a hard problem comes together, like finding gloves for a clinic when everyone else has run dry. I use AI every day, for drafting, comparing quotes and summarising supplier updates. My husband Hector fixes buses and our kids, Sofia and Mateo, are grown. We've got savings and I'm planning to finish at 65.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Picture this. This one is called AI Plateau. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine, but don't waste money on the hype. I already use AI every day, so a plateau just means my afternoons stay as boring as my mornings. At work I'd say let's keep trying new things anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us I'm calm. The tools help a bit, nothing breaks, and my pay and savings are fine. I'd be lightly bored, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep testing tools, like the one that flags late deliveries. I'd show Katrin which of them really save time. I'd also take the evening course on supply planning I've been putting off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels comfortable, if a bit flat. I'm someone who likes a bit of change, so a quiet world is a little dull.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that would still worry you here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Something I'd still worry about is dull things, like my knees and getting up the stairs at the warehouse. That's me getting older, not AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the extra time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the time to get properly good at the planning side. Junior at 58 sounds funny, but I've got a decade of pharmacy knowledge nobody else here has.

say: I'd say **don't waste money** on hype, but keep trying new things.
I'd tell colleagues I use **AI daily** already.
think: I'm **calm**: tools help a bit, nothing breaks, and savings are fine.
A quiet world feels a little **dull** to me.
do: Keep testing tools like the **late-delivery flagger**.
Show Katrin which tools truly **save time**.
S0.quote: I already use AI every day, so a plateau just means my afternoons stay as boring as my mornings.
fieldNote: Her **daily AI habit** makes a quiet world feel dull rather than safe.
Pharmacy background gives her an edge she means to use.
Real worries are physical, not technological.

steps.text: Test the late-delivery flagging tool and report results to Katrin
Finish the evening course on supply planning

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now picture this. This one is called Steady Disruption. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's what I expected, and I'm glad I started early. At work I'd say let's pick the tools ourselves before management picks them for us. Online I'd say regulation and union voices matter even more now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think my job changes a lot but I'm better placed than most. I'm junior, but I already use the tools every day, so I'm the one people ask. If a machine does the comparing, I want to be the person who checks the machine, not the person it replaces.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd offer to run a weekly session for the buyers on getting more from the tools. I'd write down what the tools get wrong, like not knowing which supplier slips deliveries in winter. And I'd push the union steward to ask for retraining hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels exciting and a little tense. I like being useful. But I'd feel uneasy for the buyers who haven't touched it and don't want to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about at work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd worry about Kofi, the older buyer who still keeps paper lists. I'd offer to sit with him, though he might say no.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What parts of the job do you think stay human?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some stuff won't change soon. Calling a supplier whose factory has a fire, and deciding who gets the last gloves, is still a human job, because someone has to be answerable.

say: I'd say pick the tools ourselves **before management** picks them for us.
Online I'd say **regulation** and union voices matter more.
think: My job changes a lot but I'm **better placed** than most.
I want to check the machine, not be **replaced** by it.
do: Run a **weekly session** for the buyers on using the tools.
Note what tools get wrong, like **winter delays**.
S1.quote: If a machine does the comparing, I want to be the person who checks the machine, not the person it replaces.
fieldNote: Her adaptability makes her the **go-to** for others.
Still worries about colleague Kofi's paper habits.
Keeps union and regulation interest alongside enthusiasm, which stops her sounding like a salesperson.

steps.text: Run a weekly tool session for the other buyers
Push the union steward for paid retraining hours
Keep making the calls on who gets scarce stock

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. This one is called AGI by 2028. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say two years is not long enough to fix anything, so we must talk about support now. At work I'd say let's learn everything we can. Online I'd say governments must plan income help before the layoffs, not after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'm anxious, I won't lie. Almost everything I do is screen work, and I'm junior. Two years is not a plan, it's a fire alarm, and I'd rather be the one who knows where the exit is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save harder, cut spending, and learn the strongest tools properly. I'd ask Meridian about a retirement package at 60. And I'd talk with Sofia and Mateo about money plans, so they don't rely on us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels sharp, like a cold shower. But I'm not frozen. I'm busy, which helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does Hector's job change your plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hector's job is hands-on, so for him the clock is three years longer. We'd lean on that. His wages cover the basics and my savings cover the rest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you write down about your own job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd also write down which parts of my job I do that the AI can't yet, like knowing the clinic managers and who needs the order right. It might be a thin list, but I'd want to see it.

say: I'd say two years is too short, and **income help** must come before layoffs.
I'd tell colleagues to **learn everything** they can.
think: I'm **anxious**, since almost everything I do is screen work.
I'd rather know **where the exit is** than hope there isn't a fire.
do: Talk with Sofia and Mateo about **money plans**.
feel: Sharp, like a **cold shower**, but I stay busy.
S2.quote: Two years is not a plan, it's a fire alarm, and I'd rather be the one who knows where the exit is.
fieldNote: Adaptability turns fear into **action**, not freezing.
Hector's hands-on job gives the household a **3-year buffer**.
Keeps a list of the human parts of her work.

steps.text: Take the strongest AI tools apart until she can run them fast
Move savings into a fixed pot each month
Drop the weekend city breaks for two years
Ask Meridian about a retirement package at 60

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now the same thing, a bit slower. This one is called AGI by 2031. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to act, and I'd make a list of who in my team needs help. At work I'd say get on the tools now. Online I'd back workers' retraining and a shorter week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us I'm uneasy more than scared. With five years I'd become the buyer who knows both the tools and the surgical gloves, and that mix could keep me employed. By 2031 I'm 63.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd specialise, to be the person who handles hard shortages and supplier trust. I'd keep working to 63 or 64 if they keep me. I'd also train the younger buyers, who'll need it more than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels workable and a bit exciting. I'd feel more in charge than in the two-year version.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your son Mateo?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Mateo to build a trade or a licence, something with hands, since robots come three years after the thinking AI. He'd say it's too early to worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you stay to 65 if they asked?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If they offer me the choice at 62 I'd probably take it. I'd keep a little consulting work for clinics if my knowledge holds value.

say: I'd say five years is **enough to act**.
I'd back **retraining** and a shorter working week.
At work I'd say get on the tools now.
think: I'm **uneasy**, not scared, because time lets me build a niche.
By 2031 I'm **63**, so the timing is kind.
do: Specialise in **hard shortages** and supplier trust.
Train the younger buyers on the tools.
S3.quote: With five years I'd become the buyer who knows both the tools and the surgical gloves, and that mix could keep me employed.
fieldNote: Plans a **niche** that mixes tools and domain knowledge.
Would take a retirement choice at 62.
Passes advice on to her son about trades, and expects him to shrug it off.

steps.text: Take on the hardest shortage cases and supplier trust work
Practise new AI tools every week and train younger buyers
Tell Mateo to build a trade or licence with hands-on work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. This one is called AGI by 2036. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long runway and we should use it for training. At work I'd say let's get the young people ready. Online I'd say unions and governments need to plan, not wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us I'm calm. I'd be 68 in 2036, long retired, so I'm fine. I'd just be sad to have a quiet end to a late career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years means I can stop at 65 with my head up, and spend my last working years teaching the younger buyers. I'd keep using the tools, but I'd also look at volunteering for the clinic charity.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels good for me and a bit worrying for the younger ones. I'd be proud of the knowledge I can hand over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your daughter Sofia?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Sofia asked about her job, I'd say learn AI now, and keep a human skill too. She works in an office, so she's right in it. I'd rather tell her early than late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do for the company or union?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use it to help the company make a fair plan. I'd talk to the union and Katrin about reskilling for everyone, not just the quick learners.

say: I'd say ten years is a **long runway** for training.
Online I'd say governments should **plan**, not wait.
think: I'd be 68 in 2036, so I'm **calm** about my own job.
I'd be sad to see a **quiet end** to a late career.
do: Retire at **65** with my head up.
Teach younger buyers in my **last working years**.
feel: **Good** for me, a little worried for the young.
S4.quote: Ten years means I can stop at 65 with my head up, and spend my last working years teaching the younger buyers.
fieldNote: Time puts her **comfortably past** the danger.
Wants to hand on knowledge and push for reskilling.
Advice to her daughter shows her practical streak, and she would rather say it early than late.

steps.text: Keep working until 65 and teach the younger buyers
Tell daughter Sofia to learn AI and keep a human skill
Ask the union and Katrin for reskilling for all buyers

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one worries me most, because it's the only one without time to prepare. What would help is real retraining paid for by someone other than us, a union at the table, and an honest company. And clear dates, so I know when to leave.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that being adaptable isn't the same as being safe. I'd rather learn the tool and fight for fair rules than stand in the doorway and pretend the machine isn't coming.

headlineQuote: I'd rather learn the tool and fight for fair rules than stand in the doorway and pretend the machine isn't coming.
portrait: **Iris Garcia**, 58, a junior buyer of medical supplies at Meridian, who came from pharmacy work six years ago.
She uses **AI every day**, likes change, and still backs unions and regulation.
With strong savings and Hector's hands-on job, she can **plan** rather than panic.
Moods stay **calm** in most cases, rising to anxious only in the 2-year case.
biggestWorry: The **2028 case**, because it leaves no time to prepare.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid retraining**, a union at the table and an honest company.
Clear **dates**, so she knows when to leave.
